questions.prompt: Chapter 2 lists the three classic security properties a cryptographic hash function is expected to provide. Which of the options below is NOT one of those three properties?
questions.explanation: A hash function is expected to provide pre-image resistance, second pre-image resistance, and collision resistance. Forward secrecy is a property of certain key-exchange protocols and has nothing to do with the hash itself.

questions.prompt: SHA-2 can be used to hash secret values directly with no extra precaution, because it offers the same security properties as SHA-3.
questions.explanation: SHA-2 is a Merkle-Damgard construction and is vulnerable to length-extension attacks when applied to a secret. The chapter recommends SHA-3 (or a MAC such as HMAC, covered in chapter 3) when a secret is being hashed.

questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why chapter 2 sets 256 bits as the minimum recommended digest size for a cryptographic hash function.
questions.modelAnswer: The chapter aims for 128 bits of security against collisions, and the birthday bound says that collisions in an N-bit digest can be found after roughly 2^(N/2) hash evaluations. To leave 128 bits of effective collision resistance, the digest must be at least 256 bits.
rubric: Mentions the birthday bound (or birthday paradox / 2^(N/2) collisions in an N-bit space)
Identifies the security target as roughly 128 bits of collision resistance
Concludes that the digest size must be at least 256 bits to provide that target
questions.explanation: Halving the bit length is a property of the birthday attack on collision resistance. 256-bit output is the smallest size that still leaves a comfortable 128-bit margin for symmetric-strength security.

questions.prompt: Chapter 2 introduces SHA-2 and SHA-3 as the two recommended hash function families. Briefly contrast the underlying constructions of SHA-2 and SHA-3, and name one practical consequence of that difference that the chapter calls out.
questions.modelAnswer: SHA-2 is built on the Merkle-Damgard construction (iterating a compression function over padded input blocks), while SHA-3 is built on a sponge construction (absorbing input by XOR-ing it into a permutation state and then squeezing out a digest). A practical consequence: a length-extension attack works against SHA-2 when it is applied to a secret, but the sponge construction immunizes SHA-3 against that attack, so SHA-3 is the right pick when a secret is being hashed directly.
rubric: Identifies SHA-2 as a Merkle-Damgard construction (or describes iterating a compression function over message blocks)
Identifies SHA-3 as a sponge construction (or describes absorb/squeeze with a permutation)
Names length-extension as the difference, OR notes that SHA-3 is safe to hash secrets while SHA-2 is not
Conclusion is correct: SHA-3 (not SHA-2) is preferred when hashing secrets
questions.explanation: The two designs are structurally different. The chapter highlights that the sponge construction sidesteps the length-extension weakness inherent in iterated Merkle-Damgard, which is why SHA-3 was preferred for the standard refresh and is fine to apply to secret inputs.

questions.prompt: What is the SHA-256 digest of the three-character ASCII string `abc` (no trailing newline), expressed in lowercase hex? This is the canonical SHA-256 example used in NIST FIPS 180-4 Appendix B and is recomputable with any standard SHA-256 implementation, e.g. `printf 'abc' | openssl dgst -sha256`.
questions.explanation: SHA-256 of `abc` is the most widely cited test vector for the algorithm and is fixed by the standard. Computing it with the openssl CLI shown in the chapter (or any other SHA-256 implementation) reproduces this exact 64-character hex digest.
